analysis.one_liner: Phases in a national standard requiring all new passenger cars sold to be zero-emission by 2035.
analysis.headline: A bill to require half of new cars sold to be zero-emission by 2025 and all of them by 2035 died in committee without a single hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the EPA to set a national zero-emission vehicle standard: starting with model year 2025, car makers would have to sell 50% zero-emission vehicles (full battery or fuel-cell cars, with partial credit for plug-in hybrids), rising 5 percentage points a year until 100% in 2035. After 2035, only zero-emission passenger cars could be manufactured. Makers who fell short could buy or trade credits from makers who exceeded the target, or pay a civil penalty into the Highway Trust Fund.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near busy roads and breathe tailpipe pollution would get cleaner air as gasoline cars are phased out. Households would save on fuel over time as electric cars replace gasoline ones. Manufacturers already building electric vehicles — and any company that earns credits by exceeding the targets — would gain a new revenue stream selling credits to slower-moving competitors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, people near busy roads, EV makers

how_it_helps.text: Sets a hard national schedule — 50% zero-emission new-car sales by model year 2025, rising to 100% by 2035 — so the switch away from gasoline cars could not be quietly delayed by any administration.

Reduces tailpipe pollution: after 2035 the EPA must enjoin manufacture of any passenger vehicle that is not zero-emission, and the standard covers all criteria pollutants, precursors, and greenhouse gases.

Creates a tradeable credit market: each zero-emission vehicle sold earns its maker one credit, and plug-in hybrids earn partial credits, so companies that move fastest on electric vehicles profit from companies that lag.
Leaves stronger state rules in place — it explicitly preserves state authority to set their own emissions and zero-emission vehicle standards under sections 177 and 209 of the Clean Air Act.
Imposes real teeth: a manufacturer that misses its quota owes a civil penalty equal to twice the value of the missing credits, deposited into the Highway Trust Fund.

analysis.who_pays: Traditional automakers would bear the main cost: retooling their lineups to hit a 50% zero-emission sales quota within five years, buying credits from rivals, or paying penalties. Gasoline producers and refiners would lose demand as the car fleet electrifies. Car buyers could face higher prices for new vehicles in the early years while supply chains catch up.

drawbacks.text: The ramp is extremely steep — jumping to 50% zero-emission sales by 2025, five years after enactment, would force costly, fast retooling and could raise new-car prices for working families in the near term.

The credit-trading design lets a manufacturer comply entirely by buying credits instead of selling electric cars, so in the early years zero-emission vehicles could fall short of the headline percentages while credit value concentrates with a few makers.

The bill text contains no funding for charging stations, no purchase incentives for buyers, and no affordability provisions — the burden of the transition on drivers and dealers is left to other laws.
Small manufacturers selling at least 100 vehicles a year are covered, though the 100-vehicle threshold keeps very small or specialty builders out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered large, permanent gains on air quality and climate by giving the gasoline car an end date, and its penalties and state-authority preservation gave it real force. But its design had genuine costs an honest supporter would concede: the 2025 target of 50% was far more aggressive than any comparable mandate, and the credit market could let automakers pay rather than change, softening the early targets. The lack of any charging or affordability funding left the consumer side of the transition unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late October 2020 and sent to the Senate environment committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the Zero-Emission Vehicles Act of 2020 on October 20, 2020, joined by four cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no vote — appears in the record before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill had only been on paper for about ten weeks of a lame-duck session when it died, with a presidential election pending and the chamber's agenda controlled by the other party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Legacy automakers and gasoline producers are better off: no national zero-emission sales quota, credit market, or 2035 end date for gasoline cars took effect, and no compliance costs or penalties were imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Legacy automakers and the oil industry

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and guided it into the Senate record on October 20, 2020.

for.name: Sens. Whitehouse, Warren, and Booker (D) and Sen. Sanders (I)

against.name: Sen. John Barrasso
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee to which the bill was referred, took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never left committee.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters were Democrats plus Independent Bernie Sanders; not a single Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired committee that received the bill never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill forced a steep shift: 50% of new-car sales zero-emission by 2025 and 100% by 2035, with penalties at twice the value of any credit shortfall. Makers with thin electric lineups would have had to buy credits from rivals or pay up. Avoiding that cost is the main reason the industry's position ran against the bill's clean-air benefits for the public.

A binding national end date for gasoline passenger cars shrinks gasoline demand permanently. The industry's interest in the bill's defeat ran against the cleaner air and lower fuel costs the mandate would have delivered.

Every zero-emission vehicle sold earns a credit, and credits can be sold, transferred, or exchanged — turning fast EV rollout into direct revenue from slower competitors. Their gain came alongside the public's gain in cleaner vehicles.
